---
title: Effects of Dietary Caffeine on Climbing Behavior in Drosophila
short_title: Caffeine and Climbing in Drosophila
abstract: |
    Caffeine is widely consumed, yet its effects on movement in small model organisms remain
    unevenly described. We reared wild-type Drosophila melanogaster on standard medium containing
    caffeine at four concentrations and measured climbing performance with a negative geotaxis
    assay after ten days. Each condition used eight vials of ten flies, and every vial was tested
    three times on separate days by an observer who did not know the condition. Flies on the two
    highest concentrations climbed significantly more slowly than controls, and the effect grew
    with dose in a roughly linear way across the range we tested. Survival over the same period
    did not differ between groups, which suggests that the change in climbing reflects an effect
    on behavior rather than general poor health. Body mass was also unchanged. We discuss
    oxidative stress as one possible explanation, since caffeine can raise levels of reactive
    oxygen species in insect tissue, and we outline a follow-up experiment using an antioxidant
    supplement to test it directly. These results add a simple, low-cost behavioral measure to
    the existing work on caffeine in flies and could be repeated in a school laboratory with
    common equipment and a modest budget over a few weeks of work by a small team.
---

## Introduction

Caffeine affects movement in many animals [@smith_caffeine_2020]. Its effect on oxidative stress
is less clear, though ROS levels are known to rise at high doses.

## Results

Climbing speed fell as the dose rose (@Figure_1), while survival was unchanged (@Table_1).

```{figure} images/fig1.png
:align: center

Climbing speed after ten days on each diet. Bars show mean ± SEM, n = 8 vials per group.
```

```{table} Survival after ten days on each diet.
:align: center

| Diet | Survival |
|---|---|
| Control | 96% |
| 0.05% caffeine | 95% |
```

## Discussion

The effect grew with dose, consistent with earlier work [@smith_caffeine_2020].
